# Introduction

Consider the problem of using a surrogate to estimate the average level in a group or the difference in levels between two groups, when the cost of obtaining the actual outcome is high.
If the surrogate is sysematically off, the estimated level or difference could be off as well.
Mozer & Miratrix (CITE THIS) present a method for selecting a random sample of the units and coding them with the actual outcome, and using the differences between surrogate and actual for the subsample to bias correct.
Mozer, Pashley & Miratrix (2026) extends this to allow for stratified sampling in order to increase precision of the final estimate.
This package provides the code to implement the methods in these works.

In this vignette, we provide an overview of the `stratsampling` package.
It first implements stratified sampling to select which of a selected subset of a population should be hand coded.
One those selected elements are coded, this package also provides estimators that debias estimates by combining an estimate based on a surrogate outcome with a bias adjustment from the hand-coded outcomes.

To use this package, first load it after installing it from GitHub (you may need to install `devtools` from CRAN to make the following code run, and you only need to run the install line once as it will install it permanently on your computer):

```{r setup, eval=FALSE}
devtools::github_install("https://github.com/lmiratrix/stratsampling")
library(stratsampling)
```

To illustrate the package, say you have a dataset of an RCT where you have a machine-coded outcome that is a proxy for some outcome that would be expensive to obtain.
For example, you might have data that look like this:

```{r}
data( toy_data )
toy_data
```

In this toy dataset, we have three baseline variables (`X1`, `X2`, and `X3`) and our surrogate `Yhat`.
`X3` is known to be highly predictive of the actual outcome.
We also have treatment assignent `Tx` and a unique ID for each observation `ID`.


# Create candidate stratifications

Given the data, the first step is to decide how to stratify.
Given a set of variables, the `create_stratification_candidates()` function creates a large number of candidate stratifications based on different combinations of the variables and different numbers of strata.
It evaluates them based on proxies for bias and variance within strata:

```{r}
candidates <- create_stratification_candidates( toy_data, 
                                                vars = c("Yhat", "X1", "X2", "X3"),
                                                Z = "Tx" )
length( candidates )

# Evaluate all candidates
comparison_precoding <- compare_stratifications_precoding( toy_data, 
                                                           candidates,
                                                           Z = "Tx" ) 
head( comparison_precoding )
```

The results are sorted by promise, with the best choice at top.
We might select `Yhat_quintiles` as our choice, but given subject matter expertise we might also choose a different one that we believe is worth focusing on.
For example, in this case, we know that `X3` is a strong predictor of how well we are able to predict the outcome, so we might include it.
We could directly use `Yhat_X3_3x3` as our choice, or we could use the `make_interaction_strata()` function to make a custom stratification that is based on the interaction of `Yhat` and `X3`.

Here we decide to make a 3 x 3 stratification of `Yhat` and `X3`:

```{r}
toy_data$strata <- make_interaction_strata( x1 = toy_data$Yhat, 
                                            n1 = 3, 
                                            var_name1 = "Yhat",
                                            x2 = toy_data$X3, 
                                            n2 = 3, 
                                            var_name2 = "X3",
                                            z_vec = toy_data$Tx)

alt_strat <- candidates[[ 'Yhat_X3_3x3' ]]

# See, same thing:
all.equal( toy_data$strata, alt_strat )
```

We can then take a stratified sample from our full dataset to identify the documents for hand coding:

```{r}
toy_data$sample = generate_sample_index( toy_data, 100,
                                         Z = "Tx", strata = "strata",
                                         seed = 4044 )

table( toy_data$strata, toy_data$sample )
```
Note our 9 strata with around 10% of the documents being coded in each.
The code will attempt to sample proportional to strata size, unless told otherwise.

Sample taken, the next step is to go and code the identified documents.
Here is a code snippit to makes a coding sheet:
```{r, eval=FALSE}
sheet <- toy_data %>%
  filter( sample == 1 ) %>%
  dplyr::select( ID ) %>%
  mutate( Yobs = NA ) %>%
  arrange( ID )
write_csv( sheet, "coding_sheet.csv" )
```

After making the sheet, go and code the identified documents using whatever robust human-coding process is deemed appropriate.
Here is a (fake) finished coded file for demonstration purposes:

```{r}
data( "toy_data_coded" )
toy_data_coded
```

Once the coded data are in hand, merge the original dataset with the coded subset:

```{r}

full_data <- toy_data %>%
    left_join( toy_data_coded, by = "ID" ) 
full_data

# Make sure we coded all the targeted documents
table( full_data$sample, !is.na( full_data$Yobs ) )
```

We can look at some summary statistics to get a sense of whether the strata are different:

```{r}
sum_stat <- full_data %>%
  group_by( strata ) %>%
  summarise( n = n(),
             n_code = sum(sample),
             mean_Yhat = mean( Yhat ),
             mean_Y = mean( Yobs, na.rm=TRUE ),
             bias = mean_Yhat - mean_Y,
             err = sd( Yobs - Yhat, na.rm=TRUE ) ) %>%
  arrange( -mean_Yhat )
sum_stat
```

We can even plot to see trends:
```{r}
sum_stat <- sum_stat %>%
  separate( strata, into = c("Yhat_strat", "X3_strat"), sep = " / " ) %>%
  mutate( Yhat_strat = factor( Yhat_strat,
                               levels = c( "Low Yhat", "Med Yhat", "High Yhat" ) ) )
sum_stat <- sum_stat %>%
  pivot_longer( cols=c(bias, err),
                names_to = "stat", values_to = "val" )

ggplot( sum_stat, aes( Yhat_strat, val, 
                       col=X3_strat, group=X3_strat ) ) +
  facet_wrap( ~ stat ) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line( ) +
  geom_hline( yintercept = 0 ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

We estimate the treatment effect using the `estimate_treatment_effect()` function, which implements the bias-correction estimator described in our paper.

```{r}
es = est_ma_strat( data = full_data,
                   Yobs = "Yobs",
                   Z = "Tx",
                   S = "sample",
                   strata = "strata",
                   Yhat = "Yhat" )
es
```

Our primary numbers are `est` for our estimated ATE and `SEhat` for the associated standard error.


# Power calculations

We can also make power curves. To do so we would need design parameters, e.g. from pilot data:

```{r}
# Using pilot data
R2s = estimate_R2( full_data, Yobs = "Yobs", Yhat = "Yhat", 
                   Z = "Tx", strata = "strata" )
R2s
```

Once we have them, we can do some calculations via `plot_power_curve()`, which also gives a table of the minimum detectable effect size (MDES) for stratified vs. simple random sample:

```{r, messages=FALSE}
target_MDES = 0.25
pp <- plot_power_curve( nrow(full_data), mean(full_data$Tx), 1,
                        R2_ML = R2s$R2_ML, R2_strat=R2s$R2_strat ) 

tbl <- attr( pp, "table" )
tbl

# Locate where curves cross target MDES
crosses = tbl %>%
  group_by( Method ) %>%
  filter( abs(MDES-target_MDES) == min(abs(MDES-target_MDES)))
crosses

# Compare the gain from stratifiaction
crosses$h[[1]] / crosses$h[[2]]

# Plot the curve
pp <- pp +
  geom_hline( yintercept = target_MDES, lty=3 ) +
  geom_vline( xintercept = crosses$h ) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks=seq(0,0.3,by=0.05)) + 
  expand_limits( y = 0 ) 
pp
```




# Supplement: The simulation support code

We also have code for generating fake data for running simulation studies of these kinds of stratification methods.
Here is an example of generating a population of potential outcomes, strata, and surrogate outcomes with the `generate_population()` function:

```{r}
library( stratsampling )

set.seed( 4044 )
dat = generate_population(N=1000, n_strat=4, 
                          bias = "large",
                          strata_config ="unbalanced",
                          tau = 2, R2_target = 0.8,
                          residual_var = "heterogeneous" )
ggplot( dat, aes(x=interaction(strata,Z), y=Yhat, color=Z)) + 
  geom_boxplot()
```


# Supplement: Optimal stratification

If we have some way to assess variation within strata, we can optimize how many units we should sample within the strata.
For example, we can see how many we should sample within each stratum to minimize the variance of our estimator using the `optimize_stratified_sample()` function.

Here we do it with the generated strata for our simulated data from above.
Unfortunately, this uses the full set of real outcomes--to do it in practice you would need a good proxy.
See the paper for further discussion.

```{r}
calc_optimal_allocation_oracle( dat, 100,
                                Z = "Z",
                                strata = "strata",
                                Yobs = "Yobs",
                                Yhat = "Yhat",
                                return_counts = TRUE)
```
